C3. Dior Lineage: Every significant Dior piece is given a lineage record covering its atelier, first owner and repairs. Tapping together becomes a gesture of reconnection with a friend, a neighbour, a former colleague or a relative.

Client topic: loneliness

Four candidate campaign directions were written for this brief. Candidate C1 was chosen and then developed into the final proposal below.

C1. The Slow Lane: Mastercard, the brand that made paying take a fraction of a second, deliberately gives time back. Participating local shops and cafés create a marked 'Slow Lane': a counter or till with no queue pressure, a stool, and staff happy to chat. The terminal says 'Take your time' while the transaction completes instantly. The message: speed is for when you need it, time is for when you don't.

C2. Table for More: Reframe the 'table for one'. When a solo diner pays with Mastercard at participating restaurants, they receive a 'plus-one' token. They can pass it to anyone (a neighbour, a colleague, a drifted friend) for a covered seat next time. Eating alone becomes the start of an invitation instead of the end of one.

C3. Next One's On Me: Lower the cost of reaching out. Any Mastercard holder can send a friend they've drifted from a small 'first round is on me' gift (a coffee, a walk-and-snack, a pint) attached to a short message. The gift removes the awkwardness and the cost of the ask, so reconnecting feels easy.

C4. Lonely Hours Map: Use aggregated, anonymised spending patterns from the Mastercard Economics Institute to identify times and places where social activity drops (Sunday afternoons, certain neighbourhoods, winter evenings). Then seed free or subsidised community moments there, such as pop-up communal tables or open-door events with local businesses.

Final proposal:
Title: The Slow Lane
Mastercard made paying take a fraction of a second. Now it gives time back. In participating local shops and cafés, a marked Slow Lane offers an unhurried counter, a stool, and staff happy to chat. The terminal reads 'Take your time' while the payment still completes instantly. The campaign owns the paradox openly: speed is for when you need it, time is for when you don't. Merchants opt in with a simple kit, no scripts, and no mention of loneliness, so it's for everyone. Client topic: repair and reuse

Four candidate campaign directions were written for this brief. Candidate C3 was chosen and then developed into the final proposal below.

Candidates:
C1. Lineage: Every Dior piece gets a lifetime provenance record. When a bag or garment is repaired, resold or passed on, the atelier records the new chapter and a small discreet mark or name tag is stitched inside next to the previous owner's. A Lady Dior becomes a piece with a biography, not a product with an expiry date.

C2. Petites Mains, Open Hands: Dior opens its ateliers' knowledge to the public. Dior artisans teach repair skills through pop-up workshops and short films, covering how to darn, reline, re-stitch and re-hem, for any garment from any brand. The new luxury is knowing how to look after what you own.

C3. The New Look, Again: For the New Look's 80th anniversary, Dior inverts its 1947 gesture. Then, abundance answered scarcity. Now, the radical luxury is what already exists. Dior invites people to submit a garment they cannot let go of, with its story, and the atelier remakes a selection into couture pieces, documented from first cut to final fitting. The anniversary show closes with the remade pieces worn by their original owners.

C4. The Visible Mend: Dior creates a signature repair mark: a recognisable thread, stitch pattern or embroidered detail that atelier hands add whenever a piece is mended. Wear becomes a badge of devotion, and a mended Dior becomes more prestigious than a pristine one. Campaign imagery celebrates tears, scuffs and darns as beautiful, in the spirit of kintsugi but with couture precision.

Final proposal:
Title: The New Look, Again
In 1947, Dior answered scarcity with abundance. For the New Look's 80th anniversary, it answers abundance with what already exists. Dior invites people to submit a garment they cannot let go of, with its story. The atelier remakes a selection into couture, filmed from first cut to final fitting, each piece carrying an optional signature stitch and a record of its story. A few non-Dior garments are welcome. The anniversary show closes with the remade pieces worn by their original owners. On the same day, boutiques launch a Dior repair and alteration service, so the couture is the showcase, not the whole offer. Short atelier films show the hands behind it all.

Brand: Canva
Client topic: the first paycheck

Four candidate campaign directions were written for this brief. Candidate C4 was chosen and then developed into the final proposal below.

Candidates:
C1. Welcome to Payday: the HR Moment Kit: Treat the first payday as an onboarding moment employers can design. Canva gives HR and managers a 'First Payday' kit: a team-signed card, a short celebration visual, and a 'what your first month of work produced' recap that arrives alongside the first payslip.

C2. The First Paycheck Index: Canva publishes an annual data-storytelling project on what a first paycheck bought, in hours worked, across cities and generations. It is built from a public survey and visualized in open Canva templates anyone can remix to tell their own version.

C3. The First Invoice: For freelancers and side-hustlers, the first paycheck begins with an invoice they design themselves. Canva reframes the invoice as a professional coming-out moment, with a 'First Invoice' template series and a ritual of sending it with confidence.

C4. The Work Behind the First Paycheck: Nobody remembers the number, but everyone remembers what they made to earn it: the bakery menu, the wedding invitation, the first client deck, the logo for a friend's startup. Canva invites people to publish a 'First Paid' receipt, pairing the design that earned their first money with a blurred amount, the date and who paid them. The campaign turns first paychecks into a public gallery of the work that started careers.

Final proposal:
Title: First Paid
Nobody remembers the amount on their first paycheck, but everyone remembers what they made to earn it: the bakery menu, the wedding invitation, the first client deck. First Paid invites people to publish a receipt that pairs that first paid creation with a date and, if they choose, who paid them. The amount is blurred by default. Creators and well-known figures seed the gallery before launch. Starter templates, including a First Invoice, cover freelancers, employees, students and founders, and a thank-you tag lets people send their receipt to the person who paid them. Employers can mark a new hire's first paid work with a team version. Later, the gallery reveals the most common first paid work in each city. 'Made in Canva' becomes a badge of a career beginning.
